content.overview: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 allows a court to admit an appeal or an application after the prescribed period if the appellant or applicant satisfies the court that there was sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application in time. It does not apply to suits. It does not apply to an application under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The explanation says that being misled by an order, practice or judgment of the High Court in ascertaining or computing the period may be sufficient cause. Sufficient cause is not defined by a closed list.
content.study: Refuse section 5 for a plaint and for an execution application. For an appeal or other application, ask for the cause of each day of delay and whether the court is satisfied. Do not treat a bare assertion as the explanation in the Act.

learningObjectives: Limit section 5 to appeals and applications other than Order XXI.
State the High Court explanation without inventing a sufficient-cause test.
enhancement.definition: Section 5 lets the court admit a late appeal or a late application, other than an Order XXI application, on sufficient cause. It does not condone a late suit.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Condonation is a statutory exception to section 3, and only for the proceedings section 5 names. The applicant must satisfy the court.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Limitation Act, 1963, section 5. Order XXI CPC is excluded by name. Section 3 remains the bar for suits.
essentialIngredients: Sufficient cause for not filing in time
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 5 is an admission power, not an automatic extension. The moving party satisfies the court. The Act gives one illustration in the explanation: the appellant or applicant was misled by any order, practice or judgment of the High Court in ascertaining or computing the prescribed period. That may be sufficient cause. It is not the only possible cause, and this note does not adopt a case-law test of what else qualifies. The two exclusions are textual. A suit cannot be saved by section 5. An execution application under Order XXI cannot be saved by section 5. Other applications, such as an application to set aside an ex parte decree where the Schedule period applies, can be considered if sufficient cause is shown.
examples: An appeal is filed after the period because the appellant computed time from a High Court practice note that was wrong. The explanation can be relied on.
A suit is one week late. Section 5 is not available.
An Order XXI execution application is late. Section 5 does not apply.
enhancement.problemApplication: Classify the proceeding. If it is a suit or an Order XXI application, stop. If it is an appeal or other application, require a cause for the delay and leave sufficiency to the court.
distinctions: Order XXI application vs other applications
Explanation example vs a closed list of causes
Condonation vs section 12 exclusion of copy time
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Sufficient-cause and good-faith illustrations are statutory, not holdings.
enhancement.shortAnswerStructure: Section 5 condones delay in appeals and applications other than Order XXI, on sufficient cause. It does not apply to suits.

The court must be satisfied of sufficient cause.
The explanation gives one possible cause, not a code.
